#4807. E-quipment highlight: the highest-rated mowers on Amazon are ELECTRIC (2026)

Despite decades of market dominance, it seems like the days of loud, finicky, gas-powered mowers may finally be behind us; and I say that because – for the second year in a row! – the highest-rated lawnmowers on Amazon won’t burn a drop of gas.

The latest round of dumb oil wars are ratcheting up fuel prices everywhere while, at the same time, state and local governments continue to tightening restrictions on noise and small-engine emissions. Combined, those things probably mean that your next lawn mower is more likely to plug in than fill up, whether you like it or not. The good news is that. in addition to being quieter, safer, and not poisoning the air you breathe while you walk behind them, electric laenmowers have come a long way in terms of power and performance in just a few years. So much so, in fact, that many of the highest-rated models on Amazon, emphatic period, are electric.

In putting this list together, we looked at the average star ratings of a number of lawn mowers on Amazon, focusing on products that had at least 2,000 reviews and a four-star average or higher, and found that (like last year) battery-electric units from EGO Power, Greenworks, and Worx were among the top-rated mowers, regardless of fuel type.

Here’s the rundown, in alphabetical order (by brand).

Over the past few years, the EGO POWER+ brand has staked a claim to being the gold standard for cordless lawn equipment, thanks to its high-voltage 56V battery platform and premium build quality. The brand’s 21″ POWER+ LM2112 push mower currently carries a 4.5-star average rating from more than 2,200 Amazon reviews and an “Overall Pick” designation.

That’s no surprise, given the LM2112’s 6 ft-lbs. of cutting torque (equivalent to a 150cc ICE), and up to 35 minutes of runtime (call it a suburban yard) from the included 56V 4.0 Ah li-ion battery, three-in-one mulching, bagging and side-discharge capability. It also starts at the push of a button, folds for compact storage and skips the exhaust, maintenance, and oil changes that come along with a comparable gas mower.

With an impressive 4.2-star rating after more than 12,000 verified reviews, the Greenworks 40V 16″ push mower is in rare company among mowers of any kind on Amazon. No surprise, given that the lightweight, cordless mower weighs just 37.5 lbs. and comes with a 4.0Ah battery and charger good for up to 40 minutes of runtime, making it ideal for homeowners with smaller yards who want to ditch gas without wrestling with a heavier machine.

The Greenpower’s 16″ cutting deck is designed for (if not limited to) compact lawns, with a five-position height adjustment and a two-in-one system offering you a choice of mulching (yes) or bagging (no) your lawn clippings.

For bigger, more demanding lawns, Greenworks offers a 4.4-star push mower with a 21″ steel cutting deck that’s powered by an 80V brushless motor and ships with a pair of 2.0 Ah batteries good for up to 40 minutes of runtime with both batteries. Three-in-one functionality for mulching, bagging, or side discharge is included, too, along with push-button starting, seven-position height adjustment, and a rapid charger that can get it back to work in about 30 minutes.

WORX’s 40V 17″ Power Share mower is another strong example of how electric lawn care can be both practical and affordable. The WG743 mates a pair of 20V, 4.0 Ah batteries to deliver 40V of power, and those same batteries work across the brand’s broader Power Share lineup of tools – a lineup that includes string trimmers, power drills, and more.

The WORX mower’s standout feature, though, is its “IntelliCut” technology that works a bit like traction control in your car, automatically increasing torque when the mower hits thicker grass (more traction) and backing off when it doesn’t need the extra power (when it detects wheelspin – or, in this case, cutting head spin). Factor in an intentionally lightweight design, seven-position cutting-height adjustment, and the de rigueur options for mulching or bagging, and you’ve got a versatile little mower for keeping a smaller lawn in shape.

#4805. Battery electric, solar-powered reefer units reach their first customers

The first regular production solar-powered electric trailer refrigeration unit (TRU) in Australia has hit the road with a real customer. Family-owned transport giant Wickham Freight Lines took delivery of the revolutionary reefer just this week.

Refrigerated trailers (reefers) are critical for hauling fresh food and flowers from the farm to your local market — the problem is that they pollute like crazy, powered by high sulfur, red-dye diesel-powered generators that run around the clock, even if the truck pulling them is fully electric. That constant diesel burn spews CO₂ and NOx into industrial and residential areas alike, and contributes significantly to fleets’ carbon emissions and noise pollution at a time when a number of municipalities are moving to regulate both.

It is, as they say, “a real problem,” but Sunswap Endurance cracked it with a solar-powered reefer that can keep food and pharmaceuticals cold in transit without burning a drop of diesel fuel – and now, they have real customers.

One of Australia’s largest privately owned trucking companies, Wickham Freight Lines decided to purchase the Sunswap Endurance solar trailer units following an initial trial, running from Sydney to Brisbane and back this past summer on a route covering a total of 1,670 km (~1,040 miles) over more than 30 hours of driving.

After Wickham’s drivers finished the round trip with over 65% of the battery’s capacity still left, the purchase was a no-brainer.

“I put the Sunswap Endurance into the fleet and told the team to stretch it — treat it as a normal unit,” explains Graham Keogh, director at Wickham Freight Lines. “We were genuinely impressed. I’m a true believer. I love the technology and I’m not a true tech person whatsoever. You can just see that it’s a winner … the performance, reliability and operational savings were beyond what we expected. For a business like ours, running a large fleet across the east coast, with a heavy focus on refrigerated and cold chain freight, this technology makes real commercial sense.”

Sunswap Endurance first showed their new solar reefer unit at HVIA TruckShowX in Hunter Valley this May past. It’s compelling, insultingly simple technology and I, for one, hope this customer delivery is just the first of many. Let us know what you think of these guys, in the comments.

Solar powered refrigeration truck looks like a natural combination. Cost of the solar is offset somewhat by not needing diesel tank, motor, and generator. Majority of savings probably come form not needing constant refueling (fuel + labor), or in not needing to overhaul the engine periodically.

I would be very interested in knowing how quickly the system pays for itself.

#4804. ‘I’m Entering My Third Bodybuilding Competition at 52. Here’s How I Build Muscle in Midlife.’

“Strength, resilience, and the courage to pursue goals don’t have an age limit.”

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

When I was 20 years old, I thought I’d reached the peak of my fitness journey: I became one of India’s first female bodybuilders, and was even acknowledged in India’s national and world records book. It was an incredible honor, and I took immense pride in the discipline, strength, and athleticism it took to get there. Little did I know, though, that some of my greatest fitness accomplishments would come decades later, in my 40s and 50s.

Growing up, I always loved playing sports recreationally, and that passion for movement and competition eventually led me to bodybuilding. But at 24, I got married and moved to the United States with my husband; shortly after, I gave birth to my daughter at 29. With all these big life changes, fitness fell by the wayside. My life was centered around giving to my family, and somewhere along the way, I stopped prioritizing myself. Over the next two years, I became chronically exhausted, lost muscle, gained weight, and didn’t feel like myself physically or mentally.

Then, when I was 33, I decided to make a change. I thought back to the discipline and structure I once had with fitness and realized how much I missed that part of my life. I wanted to get back to those habits and rebuild the strength I once worked so hard for, so, I began making time for fitness.

My husband started watching our daughter after work while I began doing full-body workouts using light weights, focusing on consistency rather than intensity. I already had a strong foundation in strength training from my bodybuilding days, so I created most of my own workouts. But I also reached out to my former coach in India, who helped program some of them.

At first, the workouts were hard, and I was sore every day. But mentally and emotionally, I felt amazing; for the first time in years, I was committed to doing something just for myself. Starting then, I promised myself that I would never stop prioritizing my health again.

Over the next year, I worked my way up to hour-long workouts and continued lifting heavier weights. As a result, I gained significant muscle and lost more than 20 pounds. But the physical changes were only part of the transformation—I had more energy during the day, slept better at night, and felt more confident and comfortable in my own skin. Every workout reminded me that I was getting stronger not just physically, but mentally and emotionally, too.

As the years went on, I kept growing muscle and losing weight by strength training four to five days a week. Still, there was always a voice in the back of my head telling me to try bodybuilding again. So, at 48, I entered another competition. I worked with a coach who helped me gradually push my limits by lifting heavier weights, adding more challenging strength-training exercises, and increasing the reps and sets of my workouts. I also followed a strict plant-based, protein-forward diet (I became vegan for ethical reasons when I was 38). So, I ate lots of tofu, tempeh, lentils, beans, fruits, vegetables, whole grains, nuts, and seeds. The work was demanding, but it was incredibly motivating to watch my body transform through discipline and consistency.

Stepping back on stage again was a deeply rewarding experience, and I felt so proud of the hard work and dedication it took to get there. Most importantly, it was so empowering to show my teenage daughter that strength, resilience, and the courage to pursue goals don’t have an age limit.

I took four years off of bodybuilding since life got busy and I wanted to give my body a break from competition prep. But about a year and a half ago, I decided I wanted to challenge myself again and see what I could accomplish in this new decade of my life. My training approach didn’t change too much since the last competition—I just kept building as much muscle as possible.

In April 2025, I began my “bulk” phase, a period focused on growing muscle by increasing my calorie intake and lifting heavy. I followed a structured workout plan with a coach five days a week through two lower-body days and three upper-body days. During each session, I usually did five to seven exercises, typically for four sets of six to eight reps with heavy weight for muscle growth. I used a mix of free weights and weight machines, and some of my staple moves were pull-ups, leg presses, leg extensions, squats, lunges, chest flies, and lat pulldowns. I also intentionally incorporated pauses at the top or bottom of certain movements to make each exercise more challenging.

Training for a bodybuilding competition also means entering a “cut” phase, which involves reducing body fat so muscle definition can show on stage. So, in January of this year, I reduced my calorie intake while continuing to strength train with heavy weights. After my strength-training sessions, I also did 45 to 50 minutes of cardio on the stair stepper or elliptical. Additionally, I finished every workout with a core circuit to improve muscle definition that includes moves like hanging leg raises, situps, and bicycle crunches.

Recovery has always been non-negotiable for my workouts, too. I lightly stretched after every session, and on my off days, spent at least an hour doing deeper stretching with resistance bands and a foam roller to maintain mobility and reduce my risk of injury.

I swear by this protein powder to support my training and recovery. It’s easy to mix and has a smooth texture without the chalky taste.

These Puma sneakers are my go-to for lifting because they provide a stable, supportive base that helps with balance and even weight distribution.

I love this tofu as an easy way to get more protein. It’s delicious and the taste blends well into nearly any meal, from stir-fries to bowls.

I’ve learned that strength isn’t just about what happens in the gym. Every little habit works together as a system: how I train, eat, recover, sleep, and take care of myself mentally and emotionally. When those pieces are in balance, I have more energy, feel stronger, and perform better.

But instead of trying to change every one of my habits overnight, I took small, manageable steps, like dedicating just 20 minutes to myself at the gym. Once that became routine, I built on it by focusing more on nutrition and recovery, then eventually, I set my sights on returning to the bodybuilding stage. When I treat my body and mind as a whole, I’m able to gain strength sustainably, which allows me to keep doing what I love.

The simpler my workouts are, the more consistent I can stay with them. That’s why my coach and I work on foundational exercises like squats, lunges, presses, rows, and pull-ups. But to continue challenging my muscles in different ways, we use simple adjustments like tempo, pauses, and stance variations.

For example, while doing a squat, keeping my toes pointed forward targets my quads and center glutes. But turning my toes slightly outward helps me feel more activation in the outer glutes and inner thighs. Small adjustments like these allow me to keep progressing with simple and effective movements without constantly reinventing my routine.

For years, I was so focused on caring for my family that I stopped making time for myself. Getting back into strength training changed that. I realized that taking care of my health isn’t selfish—it’s necessary, and making that commitment has given me more strength, energy, and confidence in every part of my life. By scheduling my workouts like any other important commitment, planning ahead, and staying consistent even when life gets busy, I’ve found a way to prioritize myself while still being there for my family.

Today, strength training is about more than building muscle or preparing for a competition. It’s one of the ways I continue to invest in my health, challenge myself, and pursue goals that bring me joy. I’ve learned that you don’t have to be where you once were to start again. You just have to decide that you’re worth the time and effort, take the first step, and keep showing up.

#4803. Wellness Apps, Medically Tailored Meals Help Slow Weight Gain After GLP-1s

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Weight regain is common after stopping GLP-1 medications such as semaglutide (Wegovy, Ozempic) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound).

In fact, previous research has shown that most people regain at least half of their lost weight within 1 year of stopping treatment, with weight regain often accelerating during the first 3–4 months.

However, a new study suggests that structured support, including a weight management app or medically tailored meals, may help slow weight regain after discontinuing GLP-1 medications.

The small study, published October 7 in Obesity Science & Practice, found that participants who received either intervention regained significantly less weight over four months than those receiving usual care.

The study included 39 adults with an average age of 50, an average weight of 189 pounds, and an average body mass index (BMI) of 31.4.

All participants had lost more than 10% of their body weight while taking GLP-1 medications and had stopped treatment within the previous 30 days.

All participants also completed questionnaires at the beginning and end of the study and used Bluetooth scales to track their weight at home throughout the four-month period.

Researchers randomly assigned participants to one of the following three groups:

Participants continued to receive care from their healthcare providers, which may include nutrition, exercise, and lifestyle counseling from a clinician or registered dietitian. The type and amount of support varied depending on the provider’s recommendations and available resources. The researchers did not provide any additional intervention.

Participants received a subscription to Noom, an app that uses behavioral strategies to support weight loss and maintenance. These include tracking food intake, exercise, and weight, as well as educational lessons on the psychological, physiological, social, and environmental factors that influence eating behaviors.

The app also provides tools to help users recognize and manage triggers that may lead to overeating. Participants were encouraged to use the app for at least 15 minutes daily, including completing lessons, logging food, and tracking their weight.

These are typically nutrient-dense meals developed by registered dietitians to meet the nutritional needs of people with specific health conditions, such as chronic kidney disease or uncontrolled type 2 diabetes.

For this study, participants in this group selected 10 portion-controlled, “weight wellness” meals each week from more than 70 options, which were delivered to their homes.

After four months, participants who received either medically tailored meals or access to the digital weight management app experienced significantly less weight regain than those receiving usual care.

The estimated weight regain was 10.75% of body weight in the usual-care group, compared with 3.6% in the Noom group and 3.58% in the medically tailored meals group.

Although participants in all three groups regained weight, the findings suggest that structured nutritional or behavioral support may help limit weight regain after stopping GLP-1 medications.

“These findings highlight the benefits of ongoing support for patients on a weight loss journey,” said Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA. Ali wasn’t involved in the study.

Denise Pate, MD, a board certified internist with Medical Offices of Manhattan who was also not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are significant “because they show that obesity management is multifactorial, not only medication, but the combination of types of meals and behavioral change all play a role.”

However, because this was a small, four-month study, larger, longer-term trials are needed to determine whether these approaches can help people maintain weight loss over time after stopping GLP-1 medications.

Ali noted that research suggests GLP-1 medications are most effective for weight management when taken long-term.

“Obesity needs to be recognized and treated as a chronic condition, similar to diabetes or hypertension,” he said.

Pate agreed, emphasizing that obesity is not always recognized as a chronic condition that may require ongoing treatment.

“I feel that the medical community, insurance, and the population as a whole have yet to fully accept obesity as a chronic medical condition, which it most definitely is for a large part of patients. For this reason, I think patients should stay on these medications long term if needed,” she said.

“GLP-1 medications are highly effective tools for transitioning to a healthier diet and lifestyle, which for most people may require long-term use,” Ali added.

Pate explained that one of the goals of GLP-1 medications is to help people eat smaller portions by recognizing when they feel full and stopping when they do.

“I tell my patients from the start, this is the goal,” she said, adding that she hopes patients will retain those habits after stopping treatment.

Ali recommended maintaining a balanced diet rich in protein and vegetables while limiting added sugars and refined carbohydrates.

He added that tracking apps and regular follow-up appointments with a healthcare professional or registered dietitian may also help people maintain their progress.

“Patients need to understand that the GLP medication is not a miracle drug, although with the dramatic weight loss, it can be perceived as such. It is only a tool to be used in conjunction with an exercise routine as well as a healthy diet,” Pate said.

#4802. Anthropologie Daily Practice Review: I Tested the Brand’s New Loungewear Label

The laidback line offers cozy fleeces, elevated sweats, and layerable outerwear.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

When I think of Anthropologie, I think of its versatile wardrobe staples like denim, office-appropriate blouses, and midi-length dresses. But the brand offers so much more, from home goods and furniture to wedding collections and statement accessories; I’ve bought a smattering of SKUs from Anthropologie over the years.

However, I was only recently introduced to its newest label, Daily Practice, which launched in summer 2024. The laid-back loungewear line combines style, comfort, and versatility for busy women who do it all.

Daily Practice is Anthropologie’s loungewear label, offering styles for everything from downtime to playtime to working at home. It’s less “activewear” and more “cozy athleisure” meant to multitask in our everyday lives. Think: sherpa fleeces, sweats, puffer jackets, casual tees, and stretchy dresses.

Ahead of Daily Practice’s latest collection, Anthropologie reached out to Women’s Health to try some pieces from the launch. Over the past two weeks, I tested four styles: a fleece quarter-zip, balloon-style joggers, a mock neck pullover sweater, and straight-leg sweatpants. Since New York is having transitional fall weather, I wore each piece on its own and layered with base layers like T-shirts and long sleeves. I also wore some styles while working from home, at the movie theater, and spectating at the New York City Marathon.

Of everything in the new collection, I was most excited to try this quarter-zip sherpa jacket. A fleece is one of the best layers to have in your fall and winter wardrobe. On warmer days, I wore it with just a T-shirt underneath, but as the weather gets colder, I plan to layer it with turtlenecks and wool base layers.

The High Altitude Sherpa is super soft, easy to layer under, and versatile thanks to the side vents, front pockets, and tall funnel neck. I love that the neck zips up to my chin, so I can cozy up on cold days.

The block print pattern stands out in all three colorways, but I especially love the turquoise one for a bright pop of color and the orange contrast stitching. I opted for size small for a relaxed, boxy fit, and it fits true to size.

These laid-back pants look just as good styled with ballet flats and a cardigan as they do lounging on my couch. The lightweight, breathable cotton material has just enough spandex to make the joggers feel buttery smooth against the skin. Note: The pants are fairly thin, so they’re not suitable for freezing temps, but since they’re baggy, you can easily layer leggings or thermal underwear underneath.

I prefer the Ease State Pants when I’m working from home and don’t want to feel like I’m sitting in sweats all day. They’re also great for light movement like yoga, walking, or running errands. I’d suggest taking your normal size in these pants for that balloon-leg look—the drawstring waist will ensure a perfect fit.

Designed with a relaxed silhouette and a ribbed mock neck, this cotton-blend knit pullover feels like a sweatshirt but looks much more put together. I love the dropped shoulders for an easygoing look you can dress up or down. Contrasting ribbed trim along the sleeves and cuffs adds style and stretch.

This style definitely runs large (I ordered a size small), and I found excessive fabric around the bottom of the torso that didn’t drape the way I wanted. However, as a tall person with long arms, I appreciate the sleeve length. The mock neck is also comfortable to wear all day without itching or feeling tight.

In theory, I love these pants so much. They’re the perfect mix of sweatpants and trousers, and the material feels like a blend of track pants and cotton-fleece sweats. The straight-leg silhouette and front darts create a more tailored look with hidden pockets concealed in the dart seam. Two large back pockets also fit your phone and wallet.

My only complaint is that the waist runs very large. I wish there was a drawstring or more elastic in the waistband because they’re too large to stay up on my hips. I do like the low-rise style, which offers a more trendy look that’s great for layering, but I would size down next time. For now, I haven’t worn them out of the house since they’re too big, but they’ll be great for layering over bike shorts or thermal leggings this winter.

Daily Practice knows its audience: working women, multi-tasking moms, stylish consumers who care about looking cute and feeling comfy. If this sounds like you, the new collection is definitely worth checking out. The label has a great range of elevated basics, loungewear, and layerable outerwear right now.

While the price points are steeper than some other loungewear brands, I found that the designs have more thought and intention behind them than your typical “leggings and a sports bra” outfitter. The cute silhouettes, colors, and details make Daily Practice’s pieces feel fashionable.

Whether I’m at home watching a movie or on the go, I know I’ll reach for these versatile pieces a lot over the next couple of months. Similar to Anthropologie’s other in-house labels, Daily Practice runs large. So if you’re between sizes, I would recommend sizing down.

#4801. Michael Strahan Shares the Words That Helped His Daughter Through Brain Cancer Treatment

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

For years, Michael Strahan appeared in commercials for St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital, delivering a message he never imagined would become so personal: “No parent should have to hear that their child has cancer.”

But in 2023, the beloved TV host and former NFL player faced that reality when his daughter, Isabella, was diagnosed with brain cancer at 19 years old.

“[That] line that I used to deliver, usually at the end of the commercial…here I am actually filling that line in my life in real time,” Strahan told Healthline.

Strahan believes his longtime connection with St. Jude was more than a coincidence. After years of advocating for families affected by childhood cancer, he found himself on the other side of that experience.

“When I needed that family…they were there for me,” he said. “I’m just appreciative, and I think things come back to you; give out good, good comes back.”

In October 2023, Isabella began experiencing vomiting, headaches, and balance issues during her freshman year at the University of Southern California (USC). Tests revealed that she had medulloblastoma, a fast-growing cancerous brain tumor located in the cerebellum. She underwent emergency brain surgery, radiation therapy, and four rounds of chemotherapy.

While medulloblastoma typically occurs in children between the ages of 3 and 9, it can also affect young adults like Isabella.

“[The] biology in adolescents and young adults can differ meaningfully from pediatric cases, requiring specialized expertise at centers of excellence for this disease,” Arnab Chakravarti, MD, director of the Brain Tumor Program at The Ohio State University, told Healthline.

Medulloblastoma is sometimes confused with glioblastoma, the most common type of malignant primary brain tumor in adults. Glioblastoma is particularly aggressive, with a median overall survival of just 15 months and a 5-year survival rate of less than 10%.

However, Chakravarti explained that medulloblastoma has a significantly higher cure rate than glioblastoma.

“[This is] a point of genuine hope that deserves to be communicated clearly,” he said.

Radiation therapy is a cornerstone of medulloblastoma treatment. Isabella received proton therapy, which uses precisely targeted radiation to treat tumors while limiting exposure to surrounding healthy tissue.

“For medulloblastoma, this physical precision is transformative,” Chakravarti said. “Proton craniospinal irradiation dramatically reduces [collateral] exposure — preserving cochlear function and hearing, reducing cardiovascular risk, protecting the thyroid, and most critically, sparing developing brain tissue in ways that translate into measurably better neurocognitive outcomes years after treatment.”

He added that multiple prospective studies have shown that children and young adults treated with proton craniospinal irradiation experience less cognitive decline and better quality of life compared to those treated with conventional radiation.

Today, Isabella is back at USC, embracing the everyday routines she once had to put on hold.

“I am back at USC, so…it’s been great, in the midst of exams, so it’s a little stressful, but I actually [am] inviting the stress in because at one point I didn’t have exams, so I’m happy to be back,” Isabella told Healthline.

Along with attending classes, Isabella is enjoying activities such as working out and cooking. She continues to undergo MRI scans of her head and spine every three months, but said that after another year, the scans will become less frequent, occurring every six months.

“But really…I don’t have a lot of doctor’s appointments,” she said.

“It feels like a brand-new life, but it’s a good one. And that’s wonderful,” Isabella said.

Isabella said her family’s support played an important role in helping her through cancer treatment. Spending so much time together in the hospital brought them closer as they watched movies and played cards and board games to pass the time.

“[It] really, really bonds you to people, and just having my dad and my whole family there was something that [you] can’t beat,” she told Healthline.

Michael said that despite the difficult circumstances, he cherishes the time he spent with his daughter. Before her diagnosis, Isabella was a typical teenager who spent much of her time at school or with friends.

“They say you spend the most time with your kid for the first few years of their life, and then once school starts, you don’t get a chance to spend as much time as you would like with them,” he said.

While Michael said he and Isabella already had a close relationship, her diagnosis brought the family even closer and helped them reflect on what mattered most.

“[What] was really important was family, and relationships, and the love that you have for each other, and the support you have to give each other,” he said. “I think that our relationship now is better than ever.”

Today, Michael makes an effort to visit Isabella at USC whenever he’s in Los Angeles during the NFL season.

“Some weekends she [has time for me]. Some she doesn’t,” he said. “But just to have that relationship with your child, where they want to hang out with you, is a good feeling, and that’s the relationship that we have.”

Michael and Isabella are sharing their story to raise awareness about brain cancer and offer hope to other families facing similar challenges.

They recently participated in a fireside chat in New York City hosted by Real Chemistry and SMAC, where they discussed their family’s experience navigating Isabella’s diagnosis, mental health, caregiving, and the impact of sharing their story.

Throughout her treatment, Isabella also documented her experience through a series of YouTube vlogs and the ABC primetime documentary, “Life Interrupted: Isabella Strahan’s Fight to Beat Cancer.”

For Michael, helping others is a value he learned from his parents. He recalled how his father used his transportation business in Germany to support people in need after retiring from the military.

“[He] would take donations, and use his money and his trucks, and drive stuff to Yugoslavia and Czechoslovakia, and drop it off there at local churches and the shelters for people, who he had no connection with,” said Michael. “So for me, I think I do what I feel is on my heart and what’s important to me.”

For parents caring for children with cancer, Michael emphasized that it’s OK to feel overwhelmed or emotional. He encouraged them to show their children love and support while helping them maintain hope for the future.

“I think positivity is the main thing because it was so tough on her at the time when she was [saying], ‘I can’t do it. I can’t do this. I can’t do that,’” said Michael.

Michael said he made a conscious effort to replace words like “can’t” and “if” with “when” while encouraging Isabella during treatment.

“Anytime she got down on herself, I’d say, ‘when you go back to college, when you do this, when you do that,’” said Michael. “And I just think the positive attitude and the love that you can give and the confidence that you can display towards your loved one [or] your child who’s going through something like this is the only thing you can do because you’re at the mercy of medicine.”

Now in her senior year at USC, Isabella is looking ahead to life after graduation.

“[There’s] a lot of interesting opportunities and things that I want to pursue,” she said.

Michael has no doubt she will find her way.

“She’s so talented, and this experience, in my opinion, has opened up my eyes to more talent that she has that I didn’t realize…the talent to connect people, and be in front of a crowd. I always thought she’d be nervous because I get nervous, but she’s better than me,” he said.

#4800. The 6 Best Beard Trimmers for Men in 2026, Tested by Grooming Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Expert-approved trimmers from Panasonic, Bevel, and more.

THE FIRST STEP to a righteous beard? Grow one. Like, don’t touch your facial hair at all for at least six weeks. The second step—once you have enough length—trim it up. The growing part is easy, but once you get to styling, things get a bit more complicated. Whether you want a long, flowing beard or something shorter and cleaner, using the right beard products to keep your facial fur in shape also ensures your whiskers stay strong and healthy. And no tool is more important than a quality beard trimmer.

I’m one of those weird dudes who had a full beard by the time I left middle school, so I’ve been guinea pigging beard trimmers since before I was doing trigonometry—which, to be fair, extends to this day (is that the one with shapes?). In the years since, I have tried out just about every beard style you can think of: long grisly beard, tight stubble, even a goatee for a short period of time after seeing the first Iron Man movie (I have had all photographic evidence either scrubbed from the internet or burnt in a fire, so don’t even try).

Through this all, a beard trimmer was the most consequential tool in my grooming arsenal, with the best options changing with each style. Nothing else can give you a uniform cut or easily shape or fade a beard the way a trimmer can, no matter the beard’s style. But beyond length possibilities, you’ll want to consider your hair type and where you are in your own personal facial hair journey. For example, if your beard is coarse or very thick, you’ll need a more powerful trimmer like the Bevel trimmer or Braun Series 9.

If you’re new to growing a beard, you might want to look on the simpler side to make sure you get the hang of beard trimming before you invest, like with the Philips Norelco OneBlade. And if you’re a beard veteran, you’ll want something more professional-grade (like the Panasonic trimmer) and fly without the protection of guards. Then there are the specifics of each device (including how easy it is to maintain), which will really determine the best beard trimmer for you to invest in.

Of course, ultimately what beard trimmer is best for you comes down to your personal needs and preferences (which is why this list has six trimmers, not just one). But there are a few things you can look for that are essential for any beard trimmer, no matter what sort of beard you're caring for. Here’s the lowdown on how to shop for the best beard trimmers in 2026.

You want a strong motor with enough juice to shave or cut to the right length cleanly, smoothly, and with a minimal number of passes (more passes make for more skin irritation). In most cases, you get what you pay for here. The most budget-friendly beard trimmers in our roundup (those under $50) all do a decent job, but they often can’t match the raw power of a more premium, $100-plus model.

This is why you’ll notice most budget options tend not to disclose their motor speed, while all the higher-end devices on this list start at either 6,000 rpm (rotations per minute) or 10,000 cuts per minute, depending on which metric they use to detail motor power.

Much like the motor, the blades of a trimmer will dictate how quickly and effectively it cuts through hair. Typically, you want to look for blades made of durable materials like stainless steel or metal that stay sharp for a long time (many trimmers will even have self-sharpening blades, which is a plus for longevity).

You will eventually need to replace the blades, so choosing one with replaceable blades will always be helpful, but blades made from strong materials, like metals, will last longer than those made of plastic.

Cordless trimmers are great for a lot of reasons, which makes them the preferred choice for most bearded gents. But they can’t match the sheer power of traditional, corded models. If you’re opting for the latter, consider models with a long, flexible power cord like Bevel’s. This makes them both easier to store and to maneuver around your face with better precision.

If you’re opting for a cordless model, it’s important to keep its battery life in mind. Knowing how often you’ll need to charge it can mean never needing to stop in the middle of a trim to recharge (believe us, it happens way more often than you’d think). If you can remember to charge your trimmer often, then battery life may not be super important to you, but if you can’t, travel a lot, or just don’t want the hassle, opting for one with a long battery life is important.

Of course, length attachments are important in a beard trimmer as they allow you the freedom to customize the length of your beard with ease (and ensure an even cut). Some beard trimmers include only the most essential tools and attachments, which is fine if you’re a beginner or just need the basics.

But other, more comprehensive kits are made more versatile with the addition of things like guide combs, extra trimmer heads, nose trimmer attachments, and more. Not having these isn’t necessarily a deal-breaker; again, it’s all about what’s right for you.

I barely remember the days before I had a beard, so you could say I’ve been testing trimmers for roughly two decades at this point. However, over the past two years, I’ve consulted with my fellow Men's Health editors and writers on the best-performing beard trimmers and which they prefer. As a grooming editor, I’m constantly testing the latest and greatest beard-trimming products, so I can also confirm that this list is up to date for the best options available in 2026.

Based on this experience, I was able to narrow down our search before I put a number of beard trimmers to the test to evaluate—or reevaluate—their effectiveness, durability, price point, and ease of use. #4798. XCMG debuts new, fully autonomous electric terminal tractor [video]

The new XCMG SDA411 concept terminal truck is fully electric, has no cabin, and an L4 autonomous tech stack that’s purpose-built for unmanned logistics – and, if XCMG get their way, it looks like the future of drayage truck operations.

Whether you call them terminal trucks, yard dogs, or anything else, these heavy-duty trucks do work that’s ideally suited to electrification. It’s all low-speed, high-torque, short distance, precision operation, all the time. And the quiet, vibration-free, instant power operation of electric drive is in its element.

Chinese equipment brand XCMG gets it, and they’re taking the electric terminal truck concept a step further with the debut of an all-new, cab-less design that’s 100% autonomous.

“With no cab and an L4 autonomous driving system, the platform is purpose-built for unmanned logistics,” said XCMG, on LinkedIn. “Its 360° perception system enables autonomous navigation, obstacle avoidance, task execution and parking, supporting continuous mixed-traffic operations in demanding environments.”

That same post included a video showing the SDA411 make its way around XCMG’s campus, making some emergency stops, and pulling up to a charger for a human attendant to plug it in (I guess they haven’t heard about Fortescue’s trick with the KUKA welding robot, yet). You can check out the post for yourself, below.

As for the autonomous aspect, while I generally side with labor and humanity over management and technology, there’s some truth to the industry claims that young people don’t want to drive trucks anymore, even with the promise of six-figure salaries.

Combine that with an aging workforce and not enough new talent entering the field, and virtually every industrial sector is struggling with a serious operator shortage. Autonomous equipment like the SDA411 could help address that shortage, keeping goods moving even when there aren’t enough drivers to go around. And rather than simply replacing workers, the technology could let experienced operators oversee multiple vehicles, take on supervisory roles and stay in the industry longer, while making these jobs accessible to people who might not otherwise be able to do them.

It doesn’t have to be autonomous because it’s electric it only needs to be powered by electric motors not gas to be better in every way.

If XCMG get their way, we’ll get to see how that all plays out somewhat sooner than later. In the meantime, we’ll have to settle for hearing what you think about the SDA411 and how it could impact brands like Kalmar and Orange EV in the comments.

#4797. Hormone Therapy May Help Improve Menopause Brain Fog, Mood Changes

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Menopause hormone therapy (MHT), also known as hormone replacement therapy (HRT), helps manage various menopause symptoms.

Currently, MHT is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to help relieve hot flashes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, and dyspareunia (pain during sex).

However, recent research has found that MHT may also help improve mental symptoms like “brain fog” and mood changes.

Other research also found that MHT does not affect dementia risk. This research followed the FDA’s removal of the black box warning on these products, which suggested they may increase the risk.

Together, these studies show that MHT may help people experiencing menopause in ways not previously realized and that it is generally safe to use.

Research published in Scientific Reports on September 1 suggests that an estrogen hormone treatment that combines estriol and progesterone may help ease the symptoms of brain fog during menopause.

Brain fog may involve memory lapses, difficulty concentrating, and slower thinking.

Just about two-thirds of women experience cognitive difficulties, like brain fog, during the menopausal transition. However, there is currently no Food and Drug Administration (FDA)- approved treatment for these symptoms.

This study was an observational case series that followed 20 menopausal women with an average age of 53. Each participant was given a baseline assessment for cognitive symptoms prior to treatment.

They were then treated for 12 months with a customized regimen of estriol and progesterone.

Estriol is a natural form of estrogen that occurs during pregnancy and has been used in Europe and Asia to treat other symptoms of menopause.

After 12 months, the participants reported significant reductions in:

“Estrogen plays a well-documented role in protecting the brain, yet there are still no approved type and dose of treatment that specifically targets the cognitive symptoms so many women experience during menopause,” Rhonda Voskuhl, MD, neurologist, member of the Comprehensive Menopause Center at UCLA Health, and senior study author, said in a press release.

“Women are often told to simply live with brain fog, when in fact there is a neuroscience basis for it, and potentially a way to address it. That gap in care is what motivated us to look more closely at estriol,” Voskuhl said.

This was a small, preliminary case series without a placebo group or randomization. More research is needed to confirm the benefits for cognitive symptoms.

A study published September 9 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society, showed that hormone therapy may help improve mood changes in women in midlife.

The researchers noted that mood disturbances, such as depression, irritability, anxiety, and mental exhaustion, affect up to 68% of women during menopause.

“The erratic changes and loss of estrogen associated with this hormonal transition can lower serotonin and dopamine levels, which [are] associated with depression and cognitive changes, including poor concentration, brain fog, and memory loss,” said Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study.

The study included 260 individuals with an average age of 52 years. Just over half of the participants had a history of anxiety or depression, and 24% were using an antidepressant medication at the start of the study.

Each participant completed the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS) both before and after initiating hormone therapy for FDA-approved indications, such as hot flashes and night sweats.

The average follow-up during the study was 4.5 months. Between the baseline and the follow-up, there was a significant reduction in the MRS psychological scores. The percentage of participants with severe mood symptoms decreased from 62.3% to 24.6%.

Treatment response didn’t appear to differ by age, menopausal stage, psychiatric history, or antidepressant use. These findings suggest that hormone therapy may help improve mood symptoms in midlife, especially for those with higher severity of symptoms before treatment.

“This study supports the evidence that starting hormone therapy for the typical disruptive symptoms of menopause may bring collateral benefits, including improvement in mood,” Ross said. “Communicating with your healthcare provider is always best to manage your symptoms and prepare yourself properly for this next stage of life.”

For decades, women have been warned about the serious potential risks associated with menopause hormone therapy (MHT). This included an FDA “black box” warning citing complications like cardiovascular disease, cancer, and dementia.

However, a recent meta-analysis commissioned by the World Health Organization (WHO) that included data from more than a million women, and was published in The Lancet Healthy Longevity, found that MHT neither increased nor decreased dementia risk.

“The World Health Organisation currently provides no guidance on MHT and dementia risk, leaving a critical gap for women, clinicians, and policymakers. Our work will help inform upcoming WHO guidelines on reducing the risk of cognitive decline and dementia,” Melissa Melville, a PhD candidate and aging researcher in the Department of Clinical Health Psychology at the University College London, and first author of the study, told Healthline in a previous interview.

In the same interview, Melville stressed that the importance of this work is twofold: for clinicians, there is an urgent need for higher-quality research, and for patients, decisions about MHT should be guided by symptoms and well-established benefits and risks.

#4796. Amflow launches two powerful new electric bikes, including its first SUV-style e-bike

Amflow, the electric bicycle brand that burst onto the scene with some of the most powerful and lightweight electric mountain bikes on the market, is expanding its lineup with two major releases. The company has announced global availability of its new Amflow TL Carbon, while also bringing its removable-battery Amflow PR Carbon series to the US for the first time.

Both models are powered by the latest Avinox mid-drive motor systems, which have quickly earned a reputation for delivering impressive power in surprisingly compact packages.

The biggest departure from Amflow’s roots is the new TL Carbon, which takes the company’s high-performance mountain biking DNA and applies it to a more versatile SUV-style electric bike. While less common in the US (ironically), SUV-style e-bikes are essentially a hybrid electric bicycle designed to act as an all-in-one, “do-it-all” vehicle combining the rugged build and off-road capability of an electric mountain bike with the practical, everyday utility of a city or trekking bike.

Rather than focusing exclusively on technical trails and aggressive mountain biking, the TL Carbon is designed to handle everything from daily commuting to touring and off-road adventures. And with Avinox’s RS800 battery featuring 800Wh of capacity, it’s got plenty of energy on board for diverse adventures.

The full-suspension bike uses the Avinox M2 motor, delivering up to 125 Nm of torque, which should provide more than enough grunt for steep climbs, heavy loads, and just about anything else riders can throw at it.

Avinox e-bike drive systems are known for many things, but chief among them is the extremely high power and torque they offer, eclipsing most other mid-drive motor systems on the market.

Despite that power and versatility, the TL Carbon weighs as little as 22.6 kg (49.8 lb). It also boasts an impressive maximum total weight capacity of 200 kg (441 lb), including the bike itself, rider, and cargo carried on its front and rear racks.

That’s a compelling combination for riders who want the performance of a premium electric mountain bike but need something practical enough to replace a car for everyday trips.

And perhaps most surprisingly, the price isn’t completely outrageous. The Amflow TL Carbon starts at $3,899 in the US and €3,499 in Germany, positioning it competitively against premium European trekking and SUV-style e-bikes.

Meanwhile, American riders are finally getting access to the Amflow PR Carbon series, which had previously launched in other markets.

Unlike Amflow’s earlier electric mountain bikes, the PR series features a removable battery, addressing one of the biggest practical complaints about high-performance eMTBs with integrated batteries.

The new 800 Wh battery weighs just 4 kg (8.8 lb) and can be removed for convenient indoor charging or swapped for a fresh battery to extend a ride. That’s especially useful for riders who don’t have a convenient charging outlet near their bike storage area.

Amflow claims up to 158 km (98 miles) of range under ideal conditions, though that’s based on relatively gentle riding on flat pavement in Eco mode. Riders tackling technical trails with high assistance levels should expect considerably less. But any way you slice it, 800 Wh is a huge battery for eMTBs and should deliver plenty of range under most conditions.

The standard PR Carbon uses the Avinox M2 motor with up to 125 Nm of torque, while the higher-end PR Carbon Pro upgrades to the more powerful Avinox M2S motor, producing up to 150 Nm of torque.

In the US, the PR Carbon starts at $4,999, while the PR Carbon Pro commands $6,799. European pricing starts at €4,499 and €5,899, respectively, based on German pricing.

All three bikes are available beginning today through ⁠Amflow’s official website and its network of authorized dealers. In the US, both models generally arrive as Class 1 e-bikes (no throttle) with a top speed of 20 mph (32 km/h), though Amflow models can typically be unlocked to Class 3 performance with a top speed of 28 mph (45 km/h).

Amflow has been one of the more interesting brands to watch in the premium e-bike space, largely because of how aggressively it has pushed the boundaries of motor performance and bike weight.

But these latest releases show that the company is thinking beyond simply building increasingly powerful electric mountain bikes.

The TL Carbon is particularly interesting to me because it brings that impressive Avinox performance to a more practical platform. As someone who spends a minority of my riding time in the dirt, Amflow suddenly looks a lot more interesting to me, personally. Not everyone needs a dedicated eMTB, but plenty of riders would appreciate a lightweight, powerful, well-equipped electric bike that can handle both weekday commuting and weekend adventures.

And the PR Carbon’s removable battery is a welcome development, especially as the industry continues to recognize that convenience and serviceability matter just as much as outright performance.

With the Avinox ecosystem continuing to expand across more bike brands and categories, Amflow is also facing increasing competition from other manufacturers using the same impressive motors. That makes it all the more important for the brand to differentiate itself through thoughtful bike design, not just headline-grabbing power figures.

#4795. Many Women Over 40 Avoid Jumping Workouts—But This Simple Exercise Is the Key to Stronger Bones

And you only need a small dose of plyo to reap the benefits.

THREE YEARS AGO, at 52, Tina Tang could deadlift 310 pounds without blinking and squat 210 like it was part of her warm-up. She had discovered powerlifting in her early 40s, and by all appearances, she was the picture of strength.

So when her annual physical revealed osteopenia—low bone density—she was stunned.

As a coach who trains women over 40, Tang believed she was doing everything right for her bones: lifting heavy, paying close attention to her form, eating enough protein to support muscle maintenance and growth. But one critical piece of the bone-health puzzle was missing from her routine, she would come to figure out: plyometrics.

Many women, particularly those over 40, have been told (or assume) that jumping is off-limits as they age. “The misconception is fueled by claims of increased joint pain, pelvic floor leakage, and the idea that bones become too fragile to tolerate impact,” says board-certified orthopedic surgeon, Pamela Mehta, MD, founder of Resilience Orthopedics in Los Gatos, California.

The truth: For most otherwise healthy women, plyometrics—and jumping and weight-bearing impact exercises more broadly—are among the most effective ways to protect bone health long term, says Dr. Mehta. And beyond just helping prevent bone loss, plyometric training can actually help reverse declines, emerging data suggests.

A recent review published in Current Osteoporosis Reports found plyometrics are among the most effective tools for improving bone density and reducing fracture risk in post-menopausal women. Meanwhile, a 2025 review in BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders found that when already-active people added plyometrics to their routine, they saw promising improvements in bone mineral density at the spine and hip.

Tang is living proof of these findings. At 54 years old, and just two years after adding plyometrics to her workout routine, Tang got a follow-up DEXA scan (the gold-standard test for assessing bone density) that revealed measurable improvements, including in her right hip, the area that had taken the biggest hit, per her initial scan.

“The trend is for women to continuously lose more and more bone as they age,” says Tang. Once you develop osteoporosis or osteopenia, only a small percentage of people can regain density. “So the fact that I improved mine—and plyometrics was the main thing I changed—is major,” she says.

So even though plyometrics may have gotten a bad rap among the 40-plus crowd, that reputation is rooted in nothing more than outdated pseudoscience and fear-mongering. These explosive, higher-impact exercises deliver the exact type of loading that spurs bone growth, development, and increased density.

In sum, stronger bones, better balance, faster reaction time, and a body that’s more resilient as you age are just a skip, hop, and (broad) jump away. Here's what to know—and what to do.

“Plyometrics are a category of exercises that require you to produce a tremendous amount of force in a short amount of time,” says strength and conditioning specialist Alena Luciani, MS, CSCS, founder of Training2xl. Often described as explosive or powerful, plyometrics are more impactful than traditional weight-bearing or high-impact exercises by design.

Consider traditional squats versus plyometric variations. Sure, goblet squats—which involve holding a weight in the front rack position as you sit to depth—can support bone density by challenging the musculoskeletal system, explains Luciani. But their higher-impact cousin, the jump squat, takes the stimulus to the next level. “You have to move faster and produce force much more quickly than you would during a goblet squat,” she says.

That rapid, high-impact loading is the exact type of stimulus that bones need to remodel and grow stronger, says Parini A. Patel, DO, an interventional pain and musculoskeletal medicine physician at Atlantic Health in New Jersey. In fact, recent research suggests that high(er) impact, more explosive training regimes (like plyometrics) provide even more bone benefits than traditional strength training.

One 2023 review published in the Journal of Sports Sciences observed that high-impact jumping exercise improved bone mineral density more than non-jumping alternatives.

Bones respond best when forces hit them quickly and sharply—like the impact of landing from a jump, explains Dr. Patel. “Plyometrics naturally provide these conditions in ways that low-impact activities cannot,” says Dr. Patel. Each time you land, sensor cells in the bones (called osteocytes) detect that burst of impact and signal the bone’s builder cells (osteoblasts) to lay down new bone, she explains. Over time, even short doses of this kind of impact can significantly improve bone strength.

Just as important as their impact on bone density, plyometrics also strengthen the systems that help prevent fractures in the first place. “Plyometrics also train and prime your central nervous system, helping to increase reaction time,” says Luciani. “Fast reaction time is significant for adults as they get older because it can be the difference between tripping, falling, and breaking a hip while walking on the sidewalk, and catching yourself so that the break never happens,” she says. This is key as hip fractures have been shown to increase the risk of future fractures drastically and are associated with higher mortality rates—especially in older women.

While plyo training has benefits for people across the gender spectrum, women are especially poised to reap the benefits. Women face significantly higher lifetime risks of osteopenia and osteoporosis by a large margin. (Eighty percent of all people with osteoporosis are women, studies suggest.)

One cause of this discrepancy? Hormones, says Dr. Mehta. Estrogen in particular has a protective impact on the bones; while the hormone is best known for its role in reproduction, estrogen supports new bone formation.

Unfortunately, that means that when estrogen levels drop during perimenopause and the menopause transition, the protective impact wanes and women start to lose bone mass—and quickly, says Dr. Mehta. (Men experience hormonal changes with age, too, but the effect of reduced testosterone levels on bone is far less dramatic.)

“Women also reach a lower peak bone mass in early adulthood compared to men, providing less skeletal reserve as age-related bone loss begins,” says Dr. Patel. In addition, women have smaller frames than men, and therefore are predisposed to have smaller bones, thinner cortices, and lower bone volume than men, she adds. With that, the natural declines associated with age and hormonal changes have more detrimental impacts on women over time.

Not to mention, because women live five to six years longer than men on average, “they spend more years in a lowest estrogen state," she says, which means the internal structure of the bones gradually weakens over time, raising the risk of fractures.

Women’s comparatively heightened risk for osteopenia and osteoporosis, broadly speaking, makes them ideal candidates for nearly any kind of bone-protective interventions. But plyometrics may be an especially powerful addition.

Consider this: The spine is the most common osteoporotic fracture site amongst women, while the hip is a close second. Breaks in either area can cause pain, as well as lead to immobility and loss of independence, which leads to other complications long-term. The good news is that both regions are highly responsive to plyometric training. “The hips and spine respond especially well because they absorb the most force when you land,” Dr. Patel says.

Importantly, health care providers emphasize that plyometrics aren’t meant to replace traditional strength training, but to complement it. Strength training supports muscle and tissue health more broadly, while plyometrics deliver the impact bones respond to particularly well, explains Dr. Patel. Together, the two types of loading work together to support the health of your entire frame—and research backs it up.

A study published in Applied Sciences last year found that participants who tacked on twice-weekly jump training to their usual exercise routine had improved lower-limb joint health in just 12 weeks. Meanwhile, a 2025 review in Current Osteoporosis Reports found that high-impact plyometric exercise increased lumbar spine bone mineral density in post-menopausal women. But, the authors note that the greatest benefits often appear in programs that combine resistance training with impact loading, reinforcing the idea that the two approaches work best together.

And those widespread myths that say plyometrics are off-limits after middle age? Hogwash. “Jumping does not cause wear-and-tear, worsen osteoarthritis, or increase fracture risk,” says Dr. Patel. “When done appropriately, plyometric drills are one of the most effective ways to stimulate bone formation and preserve bone density during midlife,” she says. The real risk arises from improper progression, inadequate landing mechanics, or unrecognized musculoskeletal conditions—not the jumping itself, she says.

No matter your age, goals, or training background, it’s wise to consult a physician before giving your movement practice a major overhaul, says Dr. Patel. A clinician can review your medical history, medications, bone density status, and any underlying conditions to determine whether impact training is appropriate for you at this time. Or, if you’ll need modifications.

If you have symptoms of pelvic floor dysfunction (e.g., urinary leakage, heaviness or pressure in the pelvis, pain during penetration, or discomfort during high-impact activities) it’s worth consulting a pelvic floor physical therapist first. Conditions like prolapse or incontinence often require some pelvic floor strengthening and coordination work before plyometrics feel safe and supportive, Dr. Patel says.

Once you’ve gotten the green light, the next step is to gradually introduce plyometrics into your workouts. For most, Luciani recommends picking just one or two plyometric movements per session, performing 8 to 12 total reps of each movement, with a minimum of 20 to 30 seconds between reps.

Perform these movements after your warm-up, but before your main strength work, when your nervous system is primed but still fresh enough to generate power safely.

That may not sound like much, but it’s the ideal dose. “You want to keep the volume really low because these movements are incredibly taxing on your tissues and nervous system,” she says. “The goal is quality, not quantity.” A smaller number of well-executed reps is far more effective (and safer!) than dozens of sloppy reps.

Workout Rx: Pick just one or two plyometric movements per session, performing 8–12 total reps of each movement, with a minimum of 20–30 seconds between reps.

1. Prep your body. Your current strength, balance, bone density, and overall fitness level should dictate exactly which plyometrics you introduce first. But Dr. Patel recommends beginning with movements that build Achilles tendon strength and lower-leg resilience, since the Achilles absorbs a large portion of the force when you land from a jump. Calf raises, heel drops, and small pogo hops can all help prep the tissues and joints for higher-impact training, she says.

As you hop, make sure to prioritize two-foot takeoffs and proper landing mechanics (soft knees, send back hips, engaged core), says Dr. Patel. This will help distribute impact throughout the lower body and reduce undue stress on your joints, all while still delivering the bone-building stimulus that plyometrics are known for, she explains.

Stay here for a minimum of two to three weeks, or as long as it takes for the hops to feel smooth and you to feel confident.

2. Level up to staggered-stance jumps. When you feel stable and controlled with two-foot hops, Tang recommends graduating to staggered-stance jumps. “Start with one foot just slightly in front—the change in stance forces your body to find its center of mass differently,” she explains. The mid-line strength and increased balance you gain here will make later progressions—like broad jumps and single-leg hops—much more accessible and safer. Just don’t forget to practice with both your dominant and non-dominant foot forward, as you want to build balanced strength and stability, she says.

3. Add more explosive options. After a few weeks of symptom-free, beginner-friendly plyometrics, you’re ready to try advanced plyometric exercises, such as:

These all require you to generate even more force even more quickly, which is precisely what makes them so effective for bone health—but also why they need to be approached thoughtfully, says Luciani.

5. Try unilateral plyometrics. “One of the hardest next levels is single-leg hopping,” says Tang. Unilateral plyometrics demand significantly more balance, stability, and force production from each leg—which is exactly why they’re so effective, she says. “Try hopping on a single leg in place, hopping forward, hopping left and right.” As you gain proficiency in these one-sided movements, try increasing the distance you cover with each hop,” she suggests.

6. Don’t forget about midline and upper-body plyometrics. Lower-body plyometrics may get all the attention, but if you want stronger bones or midline, you shouldn’t snooze on upper-body variations. “Upper-body plyometrics are fun to do, dynamic, great for stress relief, and often utilize a medicine ball,” says Luciani. These exercises—which include med-ball throws, d-ball slams, rotational wall throws, and the like—help you turn, rotate, react, and produce power through your upper and middle body, which is a real asset as we age,” she says.

Luciani suggests one of your two to three weekly plyometric sessions, an upper-body or midline-focused workout. Ideally, hitting them before an upper-body-focused lifting day, like shoulder and biceps or back and triceps.

7. Prioritize recovery. No matter your progression, plyometrics require a lot from your body. Yep, even though you’re only supposed to do fewer than 12 reps per session. “You want to allow 48 hours between your higher-intensity plyometric sessions for proper recovery,” says Dr. Patel. You can further support recovery by prioritizing sleep, eating nutrient-dense foods and enough of them, and implementing stress-relief exercises.

Additionally, be sure to check in with your body. “Sharp pain, new neurological symptoms, pelvic floor symptoms, and prolonged soreness are signs that it’s time to pause progression and check in with an expert,” she says.

#4794. How to Build Your Legs With the Glute-Ham Raise

This underrated exercise could be the MVP of your lower body training.

IF YOU’RE A dedicated lifter, your lower body doesn’t lack attention in your workouts. You might even dedicate an entire session to it each week (hello, leg day). But just because your training plan is packed with deadlifts, squats, lunges, calf raises, hip thrusts, and step-ups doesn’t mean you’re doing everything you can to maximize your leg development. You probably walk right past one of the most powerful lower body machines every time you’re at the gym: the glute ham developer (GHD).

It might look like a gussied-up horizontal Roman chair, but the GHD is a different beast entirely. Instead of targeting your glutes and lower back with hyperextensions, the GHD allows you to laser focus on your biceps femoris, semitendinosus, and semimembranosus (collectively known as your hamstrings) with an exercise called the glute ham raise (GHR). It’s so effective at what it does that only the deadlift can rival its hamstring-building power, making it a formidable addition to any leg day. Use these tips to weave it into your routine for maximum results.

AS MENTIONED ABOVE, you’ll need a GHD to perform a GHR. Where a Roman chair puts your body at a 45-degree angle and only allows movement in the hips, the GHD elevates you off the floor, locking your ankles between two sets of rollers while your knees (in the starting position) and then thighs (in the down position) rest on rounded pads. In so doing, it shifts the emphasis from your lower back to the backs of your legs, requiring you to use your hamstrings to lower and raise your body primarily through knee flexion as you perform the GHR.

How well does it work? A small research trial suggests the glute ham raise is so effective at targeting your hamstrings that it’s on par with the Romanian deadlift and superior to such leg-sculpting staples as the leg curl and good morning.

And the benefits don’t stop there. In addition to your hams, you’ll light up muscles all along your posterior chain, including your calves, glutes, and erector spinae. Even your abs will kick into gear to help your erector spinae support and stabilize your spine.

IF YOUR STRENGTH program is divided into training splits, add the GHR to your leg day. If your weekly routine skews more toward total body workouts, incorporate the GHR into one or two of them, making sure it’s among a diverse selection of leg exercises spread across three or four strength sessions. Either way, it’s a good idea to perform it toward the end of a workout after heavier compound lifts like the squat and deadlift.

You can load the GHD by holding a weight plate to your chest, but start with only your bodyweight, following the instructions below until you master the movement.

In a true GHR, the lowering phase of the movement stops when your body is horizontal to the floor. Going past that point by hinging downward at your hips until your torso is perpendicular to the floor adds a back extension element and causes you to lose hamstring tension, undercutting your hamstring gains—so make sure you stay disciplined with your range of motion.

*If you don’t have access to a GHD, you can enlist a buddy to hold your ankles on the floor or use a specialized bench to perform a Nordic curl, which also requires your hamstrings to work overtime as you lower and raise your thighs and torso through knee flexion.

Trevor Thieme is a Los Angeles-based writer and strength coach, and a former fitness editor at Men’s Health. When not helping others get in shape, he splits his time between surfing, skiing, hiking, mountain biking, and trying to keep up with his 10-year-old daughter.

#4793. All aboard! Massachusetts is getting 10 new electric transit trains

The Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA) board of directors voted unanimously Thursday to approve the purchase of a new generation of battery-powered public transit trains – and they can’t arrive soon enough.

“(MBTA) has, obviously, an immediate need for locomotives,” explains William Wolfgang, the MBTA’s senior director of vehicle engineering. The new machines will replace the oldest locomotives in the MBTA fleet, GP40s built more than 50 years ago and F40s that are well over 30 years old. In a presentation to the MTBA board, MTBA said 13 of the GP40s have, “exceeded their useful life,” while the F40s will reach the end of their life between 2029 and 2035.

The MBTA will put in an order for 20 Siemens-built “Charger” locomotives; 10 Tier 4 diesel-powered hybrid electric units and 10 dual-mode battery/catenary electric units – and, beyond trackside power for charging the batteries, there are other challenges presented by going electric, most notably using existing cab cars to control the battery-electric units. “We’re going to have to work with railroad operations, engineering, and the Brotherhood of [Locomotive Engineers and Trainmen] to try and determine the best way to handle that,” adds Wolfgang. “That will be an upcoming change order once we get into the design review process.”

The total bill comes out to $310.4 million. A combination of state and federal funding will pay for the order, including a recent $200 million transfer from the Massachusetts Department of Transportation.

The contract includes an option for additional locomotives, although details were not discussed during the meeting. Delivery of the new Siemens Charger trains is set to begin in 2029, with all 20 set to be in service by the end of 2030. Siemens has delivered 440 Charger model hybrid- and battery-electric locomotives globally at the time of this writing.
